extracted.intended_audience: legal scholars, patent litigators, judges, and law students interested in patent validity doctrine and litigation practice
extracted.subtask_description: Analyze how various patent-validity doctrines (eligibility, novelty, nonobviousness, written description, enablement, etc.) are characterized as questions of law, questions of fact, or legal questions dependent on underlying facts, and the procedural consequences of those characterizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core patentability requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: The principal requirements of patent validity include eligibility and utility under § 101, novelty under § 102, nonobviousness under § 103, and the written description and enablement requirements of § 112.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the distinct substantive grounds on which patents are evaluated for validity; the article treats each as potentially implicating different law-vs-fact characterizations and procedural rules. (Text cites §§ 101, 102, 103, 112.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent eligibility (Alice two-step test)
rubrics_metrics.description: Step 1: Ask whether a patent is directed to a 'law[] of nature, natural phenomen[on], or abstract idea[].' Step 2: If so, determine whether the patent contains an 'inventive concept' that 'transform[s]' the ineligible principle into a 'patent-eligible application.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A patent does not recite an inventive concept if it covers 'well-understood, routine, conventional activity already engaged in' by those in the field. The article discusses uncertainty about which aspects of this two-step test are legal versus factual and notes Supreme Court and lower-court applications (Alice, Mayo, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-understood, routine, conventional activity (eligibility factual component)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether claimed elements are 'well-understood, routine, [and] conventional activity' is a factual inquiry used in step two of the Alice test to assess the presence of an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Federal Circuit has held this is a question of fact (e.g., Berkheimer), which can preclude early disposition if genuine disputes exist about conventionality; courts may consider extrinsic evidence about the state of the art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive concept as factual/legal hybrid
rubrics_metrics.description: The existence of an 'inventive concept' can involve factual determinations (about how the invention compares to the prior art and whether it improves computer functionality or efficiency) but may also implicate legal judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Berkheimer and Aatrix indicate that allegations about inventive components may create factual disputes preventing dismissal; yet the specification alone (intrinsic evidence) may be a matter of law (Teva). The article cautions about relying solely on specification statements to create factual disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of validity
rubrics_metrics.description: An issued patent is 'presumed valid' under 35 U.S.C. § 282.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This statutory presumption informs the allocation and standard of proof in invalidity disputes and underpins higher judicial deference to the PTO's expertise; it interacts with procedural posture (e.g., pleading-stage scrutiny).

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of proof for invalidity
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent challenger must prove invalidity 'by clear and convincing evidence' rather than by a preponderance of the evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Microsoft v. i4i (2011) confirms the heightened standard applies to patent invalidity claims, and the article analyzes tension in applying such a fact-standard to questions ultimately called 'questions of law.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Question of law vs question of fact (general principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some patent validity issues are treated as questions of law, others as questions of fact, and some as questions of law dependent on underlying facts ('questions of law based on underlying facts').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Federal Circuit and Supreme Court precedent are inconsistent; this classification affects whether issues are decided by judge or jury, the procedural stage at which they can be resolved, and the standard of appellate review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who decides validity: judge vs jury
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditionally judges decide questions of law and juries decide questions of fact, but juries may be permitted to decide ultimate questions of patent validity if those questions involve disputes about the underlying facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article discusses the historical shift toward judicial decisionmaking, the return of juries in patent cases, and how factual disputes (permitted by Berkheimer/Aatrix) might require jury resolution under the Seventh Amendment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form of jury verdicts (general vs special)
rubrics_metrics.description: A general jury verdict simply indicates a vote for plaintiff or defendant; a special verdict requires jurors to make findings on specific factual issues submitted by the judge, who then decides the legal effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Special verdicts or interrogatories can help manage the law-vs-fact distinction and reveal the factual bases underlying a jury's legal conclusion (Justice Breyer's recommendation in i4i); reliance on general verdicts can create 'doctrinal paradox' risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural posture for eligibility (pleadings, summary judgment, trial)
rubrics_metrics.description: Eligibility has often been decided at the pleading stage (motions to dismiss) or on summary judgment, but recognition of factual aspects means some eligibility issues may require discovery or trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical data show many §101 decisions are made on motions to dismiss; Berkheimer and Aatrix shifted the landscape by holding factual disputes about the inventive concept can defeat pleading-stage disposition, but courts remain inconsistent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intrinsic vs extrinsic evidence and who decides
rubrics_metrics.description: When only intrinsic evidence (patent claims, specification, prosecution history) is at issue, resolution is a judicial determination of law; when extrinsic evidence about the state of the art is relevant, factual issues may arise for the finder of fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teva explains that intrinsic-only questions are legal and reviewed de novo; the article warns that Berkheimer sometimes treated specification statements as creating factual disputes even though intrinsic-only disputes are typically legal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plausibility and pleading standards (Twombly/Iqbal implications)
rubrics_metrics.description: When resolving eligibility on a motion to dismiss, courts must assess whether patentees' allegations of inventiveness are plausible and specific enough to survive dismissal under Twombly and Iqbal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aatrix was criticized for crediting conclusory allegations without scrutiny; later cases (e.g., Cellspin Soft) clarify that plausible, specific factual allegations about inventiveness may be sufficient, but courts vary in the degree of scrutiny applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility as a 'quick-look' filter
rubrics_metrics.description: Eligibility doctrine can function to 'provide a quick-look filter to eliminate patents that are plainly invalid before the parties incur substantial litigation costs.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article frames this policy purpose as a justification for early-stage resolution of some ineligible patents, but cautions against treating every eligibility issue as a pure question of law to be resolved pre-discovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appellate review standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Pure legal questions are reviewed de novo on appeal; factual findings are reviewed under deferential standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characterizing an issue as legal versus factual affects the scope of appellate review; the article notes tension where eligibility has been called a legal question yet involves factual determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: When juries should decide eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: If eligibility contains factual aspects (e.g., conventionality, whether an invention occurs in nature), the Seventh Amendment suggests these issues should be submitted to a jury where they are genuinely in dispute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Despite predictions that juries would commonly decide eligibility post-Berkheimer/Aatrix, district courts have often retained eligibility determinations themselves; the article catalogs examples and explains the inconsistent practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and limits of specification-based factual disputes
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements in a patent's specification may create factual disputes about inventive concept, but adjudications based entirely on intrinsic evidence should generally be legal determinations for the judge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article criticizes reliance on specification language alone to create factual issues (as in Berkheimer) and emphasizes Teva's principle that intrinsic-only adjudication is a legal question.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence outside the PTO record in litigation
rubrics_metrics.description: In litigation over patent validity, challengers may introduce evidence the Patent Office did not consider during examination, unlike APA review where the record is typically limited to materials before the agency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This distinction affects what factual issues may arise in infringement litigation versus administrative appeals and explains part of the rationale for deference to the PTO under the presumption of validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inconsistency and anti-patterns in courts' treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts display substantial variability: some courts uncritically accept patentees' inventiveness allegations, some treat eligibility as purely legal and resolve it on pleadings, while others require factual development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article documents divergent district-court and Federal Circuit approaches (citing cases and statistics) and warns practitioners that reliance on one procedural path may be risky given the chaotic doctrinal landscape.
